{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Michael K. Moe''' (born November 17, 1937 in [[Milwaukee]])<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is an American experimental physicist, specializing in particle physics and nuclear physics. He is known his role in 1987 in the direct detection of two neutrino [[double beta decay]] in [[Isotopes of selenium|<sup>82</sup>Se]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Elliott, S. R.|author2=Hahn, A. A.|author3=Moe, M. K.|title=Direct evidence for two-neutrino double-beta decay in <sup>82</sup>Se|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.|volume=59|year=1987|issue=18|pages=2220–2223|url=http://prl.aps.org/abstract/PRL/v59/i18/p2020_1|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.2020|bibcode=1987PhRvL..59.2020E|pmid=10035397|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Browne, Malcolm W.|authorlink=Malcolm Browne|title=Predicted Decay of Element Seen|date=4 September 1987|newspaper=NY Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/09/04/us/predicted-decay-of-element-seen.html}}</ref> (Indirect detection of two neutrino double beta decay had been done in the 1960s.)

==Education and career==
Moe received in 1959 his bachelor's degree from [[Stanford University]] and in 1965 his Ph.D. under [[Frederick Reines]] from [[Case Western Reserve University]].

After spending a year as a post-doc at Caltech, Moe moved to the University of California, Irvine in 1966, where a preprint sent by [[Chien-Shiung Wu|C. S. Wu]] sparked his interest in double beta decay.  He designed a TPC for double beta decay, and developed it with Steve Elliott and Alan Hahn to finally see the first solid evidence of two-neutrino decay in <sup>82</sup>Se in 1987. His group went on to measure this rare decay in <sup>48</sup>Ca, <sup>100</sup>Mo, and <sup>150</sup>Nd.<ref name=BonnerPrizeRef>[http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Moe&first_nm=Michael&year=2013 2013 Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics Recipient, Michael K. Moe]</ref>

Moe became at the [[University of California, Irvine]] in 1966 an assistant research physicist, in 1968 an assistant professor, in 1973 a research physicist, and retiring in 1997.

He was also involved in the search for the extremely rare (and perhaps nonexistent) [[neutrino-less double beta decay]], for which he published a proposal in 1991;<ref>{{cite journal|author=Moe, M. K.|title=New approach to the detection of neutrinoless double beta decay|journal=Phys. Rev. C|volume=44|year=1991|issue=3|pages=R931–R934|url=http://prc.aps.org/abstract/PRC/v44/i3/pR931_1|bibcode = 1991PhRvC..44..931M |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevC.44.R931 |pmid=9967528|url-access=subscription}}</ref> in the 2000s he participated in the search for such decay pursued by [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]]'s [[Enriched Xenon Observatory]] (EXO).

In 2013 Moe received the [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]].<ref name=BonnerPrizeRef/>
